# On Mortality, Poetry, and the Pursuit of Leisure

In the state of New York, death arrives with unsettling regularity—once every four minutes, a relentless ticking clock that reduces human existence to statistical inevitability. Against this backdrop of constant mortality, the presumed importance of poetry reveals itself as almost laughably trivial. What use are carefully constructed verses, metaphors, and rhythmic musings when set against the stark reality that every four minutes, somewhere in this state, a life concludes?

This unforgiving perspective invites us to reconsider the value we place on artistic expression. Poetry, with all its pretensions to permanence and meaning, ultimately shares the same fate as everything else: decay and dissolution. All matter, all thought, all carefully crafted stanzas will eventually break down into their most basic elements, dispersing into the cosmic gases from which they once emerged. In the grand scheme of universal entropy, the poet's careful word choice matters no more than the arrangement of dust.

Yet even amid such stark truths, practical wisdom demands attention. Some axioms remain self-evident and worth stating plainly: avoid getting killed, for one. And when approaching train crossings, exercise appropriate caution—look both ways, heed the warning signals, and never assume the tracks are clear. These are not poetic musings but basic survival principles, as fundamental as they are unglamorous.

Having confronted mortality and established these essential safety guidelines, let us pivot toward more immediate pleasures. Why remain confined within stuffy, overheated rooms when the world outside offers respite? Summer's oppressive heat need not be endured indoors when green spaces beckon. Pelham Bay Park stands ready to receive those seeking escape from urban confinement and stifling interiors.

For those inspired to make this journey, the path is straightforward: simply board the Interborough Rapid Transit Company's Lexington Avenue line, which will carry you directly to this recreational haven. Once there, a variety of activities await. Swimming enthusiasts can cool themselves in the park's waters, while those seeking gentler pursuits might enjoy boating across its scenic waterways. Athletically inclined visitors will find ample space for sports and games, making Pelham Bay Park an ideal destination for anyone looking to trade the confinement of hot, indoor spaces for the freedom and vitality of outdoor recreation.

# Notes Toward Nothing in Particular

You will die. Perhaps not today, but the actuator is already turning somewhere in your chest, patient as a subway conductor waiting for the doors to close.

*Poetry is dead weight dressed up in adjectives. Nobody needs another poem about longing. The market has spoken: silence is the only honest verse left.*

**IF YOU SEE SOMETHING, SAY SOMETHING.**

Visit Bryant Park this weekend! Free chess sets, ping pong tables, and live jazz every Thursday at 6pm. Bring a blanket, bring a friend, bring your whole beautiful indifferent self into the sunlight before it, too, expires.

The body is a rental unit with a lease you never signed. Someone forgot to mention the move-out date.

*What is a metaphor but a lie wearing a nicer coat? Enjambment is just anxiety with line breaks. The critics were right all along—we should have stopped writing after the first cave painting.*

**PLEASE STAND CLEAR OF THE CLOSING DOORS.**

Central Park's Great Lawn is open for picnics, kite-flying, and the performance of joy you've rehearsed since childhood. Rent a rowboat. Watch the ducks pretend not to notice you.

There is a particular quiet that follows the last breath—not peace, just absence, the way a room feels after someone slams a door and you're still not sure if they're coming back.

*Sonnets are coffins with fourteen nails. Free verse is just failure without the courage to rhyme. Why bother? The dead don't read.*

**THIS TRAIN IS DELAYED DUE TO POLICE ACTIVITY.**

Enjoy $2 hot dogs and unlimited people-watching at the Union Square Greenmarket! Fresh flowers, local honey, artisanal everything—because summer in the city is fleeting, and so, apparently, is everything else.

You will die, and the ping pong tables will still be there, slightly damp with morning dew, waiting for hands that don't yet know they're borrowed.

*But go on. Write your little elegies. Somebody has to fill the silence between train announcements.*

**MIND THE GAP.**
outputs.L5:
# A Stranger in New York

Somebody once told me that New York City chews people up and spits them out, but somebody else insisted it was the only place where dreams still had room to breathe. Both were probably right.

She arrived on a gray Tuesday in October, carrying two suitcases and a folder of half-finished plans. New York didn't care that she was new. The subway doors closed just as fast, the taxis honked just as loud, and the sidewalks moved in that same relentless current whether you knew where you were going or not.

For the first few weeks, she was nobody here—just another somebody among eight million somebodies, all rushing between somewhere and somewhere else. She learned quickly that New York had its own language: the particular way people said "excuse me" without meaning it, the unspoken rules about standing on the right side of the escalator, the art of pretending not to notice the strange and beautiful things that happened on every corner.

But slowly, something shifted. The barista at the corner café started remembering her order. A neighbor she'd never officially met nodded good morning. Somebody in her building left a note about a package, signed with just a first name, as if that small act of specificity was its own kind of welcome.

New York doesn't ask where you came from. It only asks what you're going to do now that you're here. And maybe that's the strange gift of this city—it turns every somebody into someone new, whether they're ready for it or not.

**NEWSREEL LXXXIX**

MIND THE GAP MIND THE GAP MIND THE
CLOSING DOORS the doors do not care about your dissertation
on Whitman they close on time every time

WRIGLEY'S DOUBLEMINT chews the cud of the century
America's Sweetheart Gum since your grandfather's lungs
were pink and unscarred

*STAND CLEAR OF THE CLOSING DOORS*
the voice a woman recorded once forever
in some studio in Astoria 1987
she is older now or she is not
anymore

DO YOU SUFFER FROM
—the ad doesn't finish the question
it assumes yes
it assumes you are lying awake at 3 a.m.
composing elegies for yourself
in the style of Whitman minus the optimism

---

**CAMERA EYE (51)**

riding the local somewhere under Bleecker
thinking how every poem I've written
is a species of handrail
something to hold onto
while the train of the actual
goes on without holding anyone

the ads above the seats sell
teeth whitening / online degrees / injury lawyers
1-800 the number for what happens to you
after the doors close on your hand

and I think: this is also verse
this arithmetic of persuasion
this iambic of Buy Now
somebody got paid to write
PLEASE HOLD THE HANDRAIL
and somebody got paid less
to write "Song of Myself"
and both are equally ignored

---

**NEWSREEL XC**

IF YOU SEE SOMETHING SAY SOMETHING
say something say something say
the whole subterranean country
mutters it like a rosary

MACY'S ONE DAY SALE EVERYTHING MUST GO
everything must go
yes
that is the whole of eschatology
right there on a banner over Herald Square

COFFIN NAILS 2 PACKS FOR A QUARTER — 1938 clipping
still legible on microfilm long after the lungs
that inhaled the promise
turned to something the coroner
described in Latin

---

**CAMERA EYE (52)**

I keep no diary of the ordinary dying
just these scraps torn off the world
like transfer tickets no longer honored

somewhere an editor is rejecting
my elegy for the R train conductor
who called every station like a psalm
Nostrand Ave. Nostrand Ave.
next stop is Nostrand Ave.
as if the naming could save anyone
from the schedule

the schedule always wins
the schedule is the only immortality
we have built successfully

---

**NEWSREEL XCI**

DRINK COCA-COLA THE PAUSE THAT REFRESHES
pause
that
refreshes
somebody wrote that between two funerals
somebody always does

WATCH YOUR STEP
the tiles are wet
the whole century is wet
we are all watching our step
into the reviewing stand of the dead

and the poem, if it is a poem,
is only this:
the strap-hanger's grip
on a bar going nowhere
fast
correctly
on time

spread by men who sell smoke
for a living. I believe them
the way I believe in Sundays

to a strap
in a car

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde literary collage combining "Careful Crossing" PSA language, Pelham Bay Park tourism copy, and a sarcastic rant about poetry's uselessness.
counterfactuals.output:
# Careful Crossing / Pelham Bay / What Good Is a Poem

**LOOK BOTH WAYS.** This is the only instruction anyone has ever given you that meant anything. Not "find your voice." Not "make it new." *Look both ways*—because a two-ton Buick doesn't care about your enjambment, your caesura, your carefully wrought volta at line nine.

---

*Welcome to Pelham Bay Park, the largest park in New York City, three times the size of Central Park, a green kingdom of salt marsh and shoreline where the Bronx forgets it is the Bronx.* Come for the Hunter Island trails, stay for the fact that no one will publish your chapbook about them. **STOP. LOOK. LISTEN.** The MTA says this before you cross the tracks. Nobody says this before you commit an image to paper, though maybe they should—*stop, look, listen, and then consider not writing it down at all.*

Cross only at marked crosswalks. Cross only where the light permits you. There is no marked crosswalk for grief, for the specific blue of the Long Island Sound at 6 p.m. in October, for the way your father said your name twice before he forgot it entirely—and yet here we all are, sprinting across six lanes of unmetaphored traffic, notebook raised like a hand that thinks it can stop a car.

*Rent a kayak at the Orchard Beach concession stand.* Paddle out past what the brochure calls "pristine tidal wetlands" and what your MFA workshop would call "an overused pastoral setting, needs specificity." The salt marsh doesn't know it's being workshopped. The egret does not care that you've compared it, in your notebook, to "a single white thought." The egret is just standing there, in actual water, doing actual egret things, indifferent to simile, unpublished and completely fine with that.

**CROSS WITH THE LIGHT, NOT AGAINST IT.**
Face oncoming traffic if there is no sidewalk.
Wear reflective clothing at night.

None of this will save the poem. The poem was never going to be saved. The poem is a raccoon in Pelham Bay Park at 2 a.m.—vivid, a little rabid, rooting through the trash of your own experience for something it can drag back into the underbrush and gnaw on alone, while the actual park, the actual bay, the actual six thousand acres of protected land continue existing gloriously without needing you to notice them in fourteen lines.

*Historical marker: this land once belonged to the Siwanoy. Then it became Thomas Pell's land grant. Then a robber baron's country estate. Then a landfill. Then, finally, a park—* which is to say, everything becomes something else, is used and reused and repurposed, except the poem, which just sits there being a poem, refusing to hold anything up, refusing to shelter anyone from rain, incapable of directing traffic, incapable of teaching a single child to look both ways before she steps off the curb into a world that will not read her elegy before it hits her.

**REMEMBER:** A crossing guard has a job. A park ranger has a job. Even the Canada geese, migrating in their insufferable V, are accomplishing something—getting somewhere warmer, going *toward*.

The poem goes nowhere. The poem is a dead-end trail marked on no map, and yet—

and yet you keep walking it, don't you, at dusk, when the light off the Sound turns the color of something you don't have a word for, and the geese are screaming overhead like they know something, like they're trying to tell you: **look both ways, look both ways, there is no safe way to cross into meaning, do it anyway, do it anyway, do it anyway.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
